Series::elu¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::elu(
    double alpha = 1.0,
    double scale = 1.0,
    double input_scale = 1.0) const
Series& Series::elu_() const
Series& Series::elu_(double alpha) const

The General Exponential-Linear Activation¶

elu() applies a three-parameter exponential linear unit elementwise:

elu(x) = scale * x                                      when x > 0
         alpha * scale * (exp(input_scale * x) - 1)    when x <= 0

The positive branch is linear. The non-positive branch is exponential and, when alpha, scale, and input_scale are positive, approaches -alpha * scale as x moves left. This gives negative inputs a smooth, non-zero response while leaving positive inputs inexpensive to evaluate.

The three parameters have separate jobs:

Parameter

Meaning

Default

alpha

Sets the amplitude and asymptote of the negative branch.

1.0

scale

Multiplies both branches and therefore the complete output.

1.0

input_scale

Scales only the negative branch’s exponential argument, controlling its curvature.

1.0

The branches always meet in value at zero because the exponential branch is zero there. Their slopes meet only when alpha * input_scale == 1: the left slope is alpha * scale * input_scale, while the right slope is scale. The default satisfies that condition. celu() ties input_scale to 1 / alpha when that continuously differentiable join is the contract you want. selu() fixes all relevant coefficients to its self-normalizing constants.

elu() is out of place and shape preserving. Real floating input retains its dtype. Integral and Boolean input promote to float32, because the negative branch is fractional. The method does not constrain the three coefficients to be positive; finite negative or zero coefficients are evaluated by the formula above. Non-finite coefficients propagate through ordinary floating arithmetic. Complex receivers are not accepted because selecting x > 0 has no complex ordering.

The forward computation is represented as one fused activation operation. It allocates a result on the receiver’s platform rather than mutating the source.

Reverse Mode¶

For a tracked receiver, the local derivative is

scale                                                   when x > 0
alpha * scale * input_scale * exp(input_scale * x)     when x <= 0

At exactly zero, the recorded derivative is the non-positive branch’s slope. That boundary detail is visible whenever alpha * input_scale != 1. The exponential derivative remains connected for higher-order differentiation; the fused forward does not detach it into a constant table.

In-Place Form¶

elu_() is the in-place sibling of elu(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — elu_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.elu_();
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.86466472, 0, 2]

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0});
x.elu_(0.5);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.43233236, 0, 2]

Examples¶

Example 1. With all defaults, the negative branch is exp(x) - 1 and the positive branch is the identity.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).elu());

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.8647, -0.6321, 0.0000, 1.0000, 2.0000]

Example 2. Supplying only alpha changes the negative amplitude and asymptote; positive values remain unchanged because scale is still one.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0}).elu(2.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-1.7293, -1.2642, 0.0000, 1.0000, 2.0000]

Example 3. The full call form separates output scale from negative curvature.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0})
        .elu(2.0, 0.5, 0.25));

Output¶

Series(shape=[5], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=5, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.3935, -0.2212, 0.0000, 0.5000, 1.0000]

Example 4. Rank is preserved and integer input promotes to float32.

auto y = pluss::make_series({{-2, 0}, {1, 3}}).elu();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, y);
std::cout << "dtype=" << y.scalar_type() << " dim=" << y.dim()
          << " shape=[" << y.size(0) << ',' << y.size(1) << ']';

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float32, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ -0.8647 0.0000 ⎤
⎣  1.0000 3.0000 ⎦
dtype=float32 dim=2 shape=[2,2]

Example 5. The chosen parameters make the derivative at zero 0.25, while the positive branch has slope 0.5.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);
x.elu(2.0, 0.5, 0.25).sum().reverse();
pluss::series::print(std::cout, x.sensitivity());

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[0.1516, 0.1947, 0.2500, 0.5000]

Example 6. A zero scale makes both branches and every local derivative zero; it is a valid, if usually deliberate, parameterization.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({-2.0, 0.0, 2.0}).elu(3.0, 0.0, 2.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-0.0000, 0.0000, 0.0000]

See Also¶

  • celu() couples the parameters to keep the slope continuous at zero.

  • selu() uses fixed self-normalizing coefficients.

  • relu() replaces the exponential branch with a hard zero.
